opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the key thing is that continual learning shouldn't be treated as a special mode you switch on after training is "done." For me, the interesting systems are ones where learning never stops. The agent is always in a stream of experience, always making predictions about what's going to happen next, and always updating those predictions as the world reveals itself.

So when a new piece of experience comes in, the system should do more than file it away or bolt on a patch. It should fold that experience into its ongoing understanding, its predictive knowledge about the world. In our work, especially with prosthetic limbs and other assistive devices, we think a lot about agents that learn many predictions in parallel, things like general value functions. A question might be: if I keep doing what I'm doing, what will this sensor read in the next half second? Or how much will this joint move? Every moment of experience is a chance to update all of those predictions at once, incrementally, in real time, without a big replay of everything that came before.

There are a few properties I think really matter. First, learning should be incremental and computationally bounded. The system can't keep growing its memory and compute forever just to absorb new data. Second, it should be able to stay plastic. We've seen that many deep learning systems gradually lose the ability to learn as they're trained on a changing stream, so you need mechanisms that keep the network adaptable. Third, it should make good decisions about what to keep and what to let go. Some old knowledge should be protected, but some of it should be overwritten because the world has actually changed. Forgetting isn't always a bug. Sometimes it's exactly right.

And finally, especially when there's a person in the loop, as there is with a prosthesis, continual learning has to be a partnership. The person is changing, the device is changing, and the two are learning about each other. The system should incorporate new experience in a way that makes it more predictable and more helpful to the human it's working with, not just more accurate on some fixed benchmark. That's what makes it really exciting to me: the machine can keep growing alongside the person over months and years, rather than being frozen the moment it leaves the lab.

r001.rationale: It says some old knowledge should be protected while other knowledge should be overwritten when the world changes.

r002.rationale: It discusses updating predictions from experience but does not identify recombining learned skills or behaviors for new situations.

r003.rationale: It does not propose integrating information into an existing large language model or discuss retraining one from scratch.

r004.rationale: It does not warn about model collapse from repeatedly learning from language-model-generated text.

r005.rationale: It describes continual updates throughout experience, but does not distinguish those from inserting discrete information into an existing model.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that continual learning should look a lot more like the way a nervous system handles experience than the way we currently train models, which is to say: experience shouldn't be something you collect, batch up, and then digest offline before deploying a frozen version of yourself. It should be incorporated as it arrives, in the stream, while the system is still acting.

So the first principle for me is that learning has to be online and incremental. Every moment of interaction carries information, and a system that's genuinely continual should be updating its predictions and its behaviour on the basis of that moment, not waiting for a retraining cycle. In our work with reinforcement learning, that means things like temporal-difference learning, where you're constantly comparing what you expected to happen with what actually happened and nudging your estimates accordingly. The error signal is right there in the experience itself, so you don't need a human to label anything.

The second piece is that new experience shouldn't just change what the system knows, it should change what the system is paying attention to. A lot of the interesting continual learning problems are really about representation: as the world shifts, the features that used to be useful stop being useful, and the system needs to be able to grow new ones and let old ones go. We've looked at approaches where the agent is continually generating and testing candidate features, keeping the ones that help it predict, and pruning the ones that don't. That's a very different picture from a fixed architecture that only adjusts weights.

Third, and this comes very directly from the prosthetics work, the system has to be able to incorporate experience without forgetting the things that still matter. If someone has been wearing a robotic arm for a year and it has learned how they move, you don't want a few unusual days to wipe that out. But you also don't want it to be so rigid that it can't adapt when their body changes or their goals change. So you want learning that's fast where the world is moving and stable where it isn't, and ideally the system figures out which is which from the data rather than us having to tune it by hand.

And the last thing I'd say is that the most powerful form of incorporating experience is when the human and the machine are learning together. In a prosthesis, the person adapts to the device and the device adapts to the person, and the useful new experience is really about the relationship between the two. I think that's the right frame more broadly: continual learning isn't just a system updating itself in isolation, it's a system that stays in step with a changing partner and a changing world, moment by moment, for as long as it's in use.

r001.rationale: It says learning should incorporate experience without forgetting what still matters, while remaining able to adapt when circumstances change.

r002.rationale: It discusses generating and pruning features and adapting to new experience, but does not identify recombining previously learned skills or behaviors for new situations.

r003.rationale: It describes online, incremental learning rather than offline retraining, but does not propose adding information to an existing large language model without retraining it from scratch.

r004.rationale: It does not warn about model collapse from repeatedly learning on language-model-generated text.

r005.rationale: It emphasizes updating through each moment of interaction, but does not distinguish that from inserting discrete new information into an existing model.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that new experience should be able to change the system as it happens. Learning shouldn’t be something we do once, before deployment, and then consider finished. It should be part of the system’s ongoing interaction with the world.

But that doesn’t mean replacing everything it already knows with the latest observation. The challenge is to integrate new experience in a way that preserves useful knowledge while allowing expectations and behavior to change. If something about the world changes—or the person the system is working with changes—the system needs to adapt.

And that learning should support future interaction. Can the system make better predictions about what will happen next? Can it use those predictions to make better decisions? That’s where continual learning becomes valuable: experience keeps improving the system’s ability to participate in the world.

r001.rationale: It says new experience should be integrated while preserving useful existing knowledge, while allowing expectations and behavior to change.

r002.rationale: It discusses adapting behavior to changes, but does not identify recombining previously learned skills or behaviors for new situations.

r003.rationale: It does not mention language models or integrating information without retraining from scratch.

r004.rationale: It does not warn about model collapse from learning repeatedly on model-generated text.

r005.rationale: It advocates ongoing learning through interaction but does not distinguish that from inserting discrete new information into an existing model.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a system should be able to learn from experience as it happens, throughout its lifetime. New experience shouldn’t just be something we collect and then use later to retrain a model. It should continually shape the system’s predictions and, through those predictions, the decisions it makes.

The interesting challenge is deciding what to change and what to preserve. You want the system to adapt when the world changes, but you also want it to retain useful things it learned before. And for a system interacting with a person, that adaptation is happening on both sides: the person is learning about the machine while the machine is learning about the person. Continual learning gives us a way to think about that relationship as something that develops through ongoing interaction.

r001.rationale: It says to retain useful prior learning while adapting to change, but does not state that existing knowledge should be preserved unless it is meant to be overwritten.

r002.rationale: It does not identify recombining previously learned skills or behaviors for new situations.

r003.rationale: It does not propose adding new information to an existing large language model without retraining the whole model.

r004.rationale: It does not warn about model collapse from repeatedly learning on language-model-generated text.

r005.rationale: It contrasts continual learning with collecting experience for later retraining, but does not distinguish discrete information insertion from updates through every moment of interaction.
